name: Sydney
info: Sydney is a city on the Pacific coast of south-eastern Australia, founded in 1788 as a British penal colony on the land of the Eora, Darug and Dharawal peoples, and now the capital of New South Wales.

facts.founded: A British settlement was established at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788 by Captain Arthur Phillip with the First Fleet; the colony of New South Wales was proclaimed on 7 February 1788. Aboriginal Australians had lived in the region for at least 30,000 years.
facts.where: Around Port Jackson (Sydney Harbour) on the Pacific coast of south-eastern Australia, in a coastal basin between the Tasman Sea and the Blue Mountains, in New South Wales.
facts.known: The Gadigal and the other clans of the Eora; the First Fleet of 1788; a penal colony and then the capital of New South Wales; the smallpox of 1789; the resistance of Pemulwuy; the Rum Rebellion; the Harbour Bridge; the Opera House
facts.today: Sydney is the capital of the state of New South Wales and the largest city in Australia.

t: Aboriginal peoples had lived around Port Jackson for at least 30,000 years before the First Fleet landed at Sydney Cove in 1788 and founded a penal colony; smallpox in 1789 killed about half the Aboriginal population of the region.
The convict town became a city in 1842, grew on the wealth of the gold rushes of the 1850s, and became the capital of the state of New South Wales when the colonies federated in 1901.
After the Second World War mass migration changed the city, and by 2021 over 40 per cent of its people had been born overseas.
dyk: The first Aboriginal people to live continuously in the new settlement were survivors of the Sydney clans, who came in under Bennelong in November 1790, after smallpox had killed about half the Aboriginal population of the region.
ev: James Cook lands at Botany Bay and meets the Gweagal clan
The First Fleet reaches Botany Bay and settles at Sydney Cove, and New South Wales is proclaimed
Smallpox kills about half the Aboriginal population of the Sydney region
The Rum Rebellion deposes Governor Bligh
Gold is found in New South Wales and Victoria
Federation makes Sydney the capital of the State of New South Wales

sections.origins:
Sydney stands in a coastal basin with the Tasman Sea to the east, the Blue Mountains to the west and the Hawkesbury River to the north. Its harbour, Port Jackson, is a ria, a deep river valley cut in the Hawkesbury sandstone and flooded as the sea rose between 18,000 and 6,000 years ago. Aboriginal Australians have lived in the region for at least 30,000 years, and flaked pebbles in the gravels of Western Sydney might indicate occupation 45,000 to 50,000 years ago.

Before the British arrived there were 4,000 to 8,000 Aboriginal people in the greater Sydney region. The coastal clans relied more on seafood and the hinterland clans on forest animals and plants. The earliest British recorded the word 'Eora' as meaning either 'people' or 'from this place'. The major groups were the coastal Eora, the Dharug inland from Parramatta to the Blue Mountains, and the Dharawal south of Botany Bay, though there is debate about which group or nation the clans belonged to. Greater Sydney covers the lands of 28 known clans. The Gadigal, whose territory runs along the southern shore of Port Jackson from South Head to Darling Harbour, call it Gadi, and the cove where the British settled they called Warrane.

On 29 April 1770 James Cook landed at Botany Bay (Kamay) and met the Gweagal clan. Two Gweagal men opposed the landing party and one was shot and wounded. Cook stayed a week and tried without success to establish relations with the Aboriginal people.
sections.growth:
The First Fleet of 11 ships under Captain Arthur Phillip reached Botany Bay in January 1788 with more than a thousand settlers, 736 of them convicts. It moved to Port Jackson, where a settlement was established at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788, and Phillip proclaimed the colony of New South Wales on 7 February. Britain had lost its American colonies in 1783 and turned to Botany Bay as a new place for convicts. The soil around the settlement proved poor and the first crops failed, so that hunger and strict rationing lasted several years until the Second Fleet in 1790 and the Third Fleet in 1791. By 1804 the colony fed itself. Phillip submitted a plan for the town in July 1788 and then ignored it, and unplanned building became a feature of the city's layout.

Governor Lachlan Macquarie (1810 to 1821) established a bank, a currency and a hospital and commissioned roads, wharves, churches and public buildings. Free settlers arrived in growing numbers, from 900 in 1826 to 1830 to 29,000 in 1836 to 1840. Transportation to New South Wales ended in 1840. The gold discoveries of 1851 drew men away at first and Melbourne overtook Sydney as the largest city, but immigration and gold exports raised demand, and the colonial government invested in railways, trams, roads, ports and schools. The population of Sydney and its suburbs rose from 95,600 in 1861 to 386,900 in 1891. It reached one million in 1926, and after the Second World War migration and a baby boom spread low-density suburbs across the Cumberland Plain.
sections.rulers:
Governors appointed from Britain held near autocratic power over the colony, which covered over half the Australian continent, with Sydney as its seat. After Phillip left in December 1792, military officers began to acquire land and trade. Governor William Bligh (1806 to 1808) restricted trade and ordered the demolition of buildings put up on Crown land, and in the Rum Rebellion of 1808 the New South Wales Corps deposed him. Macquarie succeeded him in 1810 and was the last autocratic governor.

The New South Wales Legislative Council was created in 1825 as an appointed body to advise the governor, and in 1842 it became partly elected. In the same year Sydney was declared a city under the Sydney Incorporation Act, with an elected council. The vote went to adult men who occupied premises valued at £25 a year, about 15 per cent of the adult population, and voting rights for the Legislative Council also depended on property. In 1856 the colony gained responsible government, with a parliament in Sydney made up of a directly elected Legislative Assembly and a nominated Legislative Council. In 1857 all male British subjects aged 21 or over in New South Wales were given the vote.

When the six colonies federated on 1 January 1901 Sydney became the capital of the State of New South Wales, and its administration was divided between the Commonwealth, the state and local governments.
sections.life:
The settlement began as a penal colony, and its people were convicts, soldiers and officials. Former convicts received small land grants, traded and opened businesses. Macquarie decreed that the emancipists should be treated as social equals of free settlers and appointed some to key posts, among them Francis Greenway as colonial architect and William Redfern as a magistrate; London judged his public works too expensive and colonial society was scandalised by his policy. By the 1840s the poor and working class lived west of the Tank Stream, in areas such as The Rocks, and the more affluent lived to its east.

The Church of England was the only recognised church until Macquarie appointed official Catholic chaplains in 1820. Religious groups, with secular institutions, played a significant role in education, health and charity. The Sydney Gazette appeared from 1803 and the Sydney Morning Herald from 1831. The Australian Museum opened in 1827 and the University of Sydney was founded in 1850. The growing population of the late 19th century packed into terrace houses in narrow streets.

After Bennelong led survivors of the Sydney clans into the settlement in November 1790, Aboriginal Australians had a continuous presence in the town. At the 2021 census 1.7 per cent of the people of Sydney identified as Indigenous, and about 500 identified with traditional Aboriginal religions. Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park holds around 1,500 pieces of Aboriginal rock art, and many rock art sites are still regarded as sacred by Indigenous Australians.
sections.crises:
The Aboriginal peoples of the region had been isolated for some 60,000 years and had little resistance to introduced diseases. An outbreak of smallpox in April 1789 killed about half the Aboriginal population of the Sydney region, while one death was recorded among the settlers. Its source is disputed: some researchers hold that it came from contact with Indonesian fishermen in the far north and spread along Aboriginal trade routes, while others argue that it is more likely to have been spread deliberately by settlers.

As farms spread to the Hawkesbury River, conflict between the settlers and the Darug people reached a peak from 1794 to 1810. Bands led by Pemulwuy and later by his son Tedbury burned crops, killed livestock and raided stores, and a garrison was set up on the Hawkesbury in 1795. From 1794 to 1800 the toll was 26 settlers and up to 200 Darug. Conflict returned in 1814 to 1816 in Dharawal country, and after the deaths of several settlers Macquarie sent three military detachments, culminating in the Appin massacre of April 1816, in which at least 14 Aboriginal people were killed.

In 1804 Irish convicts led about 300 rebels in the Castle Hill Rebellion; about 100 troops and volunteers routed them at Rouse Hill, and at least 39 convicts died. Bubonic plague in 1900 led to the demolition of inner-city slums. The Great Depression struck Sydney harder than Melbourne or regional New South Wales: by 1933, 28 per cent of male workers were unemployed, over 40 per cent in Alexandria and Redfern. On the night of 31 May to 1 June 1942 Japanese midget submarines entered the harbour, and a torpedo sank the ferry HMAS Kuttabul, killing 19 Australian and two British sailors.
sections.legacy:
The British settlement took the land of the Eora, Darug and Dharawal. In January 1938, as the city celebrated 150 years of European settlement, a congress of Aboriginal people declared 26 January a Day of Mourning for the seizure of their country. The Darug, Dharawal and Eora are named as the traditional custodians of the land today, and 28 clans are known within Greater Sydney.

The city kept the buildings of its colonial governors and architects: Greenway's Hyde Park Barracks and St James's Church, the sandstone Town Hall, General Post Office and Queen Victoria Building, and St Andrew's Cathedral, the oldest in Australia. The Sydney Harbour Bridge, begun in 1924, took 1,400 men eight years to build and cost £4.2 million; sixteen workers died. The Opera House, designed by Jørn Utzon, opened in 1973 after disputes over its cost and is now a World Heritage Site. In the early 1970s trade unions and residents imposed green bans on development in historic areas such as The Rocks.

Sydney is the capital of New South Wales and the largest city in Australia. It was home to 5,231,150 people in the census of 2021, over 40 per cent born overseas. Migration from the 1980s came increasingly from Asia, the Middle East and Africa, and China and India overtook England as the largest source countries.

summary: Sydney was founded in 1788 as a British penal colony at Sydney Cove, on the land of the Eora, Darug and Dharawal peoples, whom smallpox and frontier violence greatly reduced. It became a city in 1842 and the capital of New South Wales in 1901, and is now Australia's largest city.
notes: START: Sydney as a city dates from 1788 (the articles say the history of the city began with the First Fleet); Aboriginal occupation of at least 30,000 years is told in origins and facts.

DISAGREEMENT left out: the main article gives radiocarbon evidence of human activity in the region from about 30,000 years ago; the History article says about 15,000 years ago. I used only 'at least 30,000 years' (both leads) and the flaked pebbles (45,000 to 50,000, 'might indicate').

DISAGREEMENT: History says the Legislative Council was created in 1825 as an appointed body; the main article says it first met in 1826. I used 1825 'created' only in rulers, and left out the 1826 meeting. Check.

Smallpox 1789: both give 'about half the Aboriginal population of the Sydney region'. The origin is controversial in the History article only; both views attributed as the article gives them ('some researchers ... others').
Population 1926 'one million' and 2021 5,231,150 (main article, 'over 5.2 million' in both). The 1788 population (under 1,000) and 1798 (2,953) left out.
The 'Eora' meaning and the Gadigal facts come from both; 28 known clans from the main article; the History article lists further clans of unrecorded territory (left out).

Legacy: the Day of Mourning (1938) as the articles give it. Sydney Harbour Bridge figures from the History article (1,400 men, eight years, GBP 4.2 million, sixteen killed); the main article gives construction as completed 1932 and designed by John Bradfield, left out.
Japanese submarine raid: History gives 19 Australian and two British naval personnel killed (21, as the main article says).
